recentItems.title: Oral History of Andy Hertzfeld Part 1 of 2
recentItems.description:
Interviewed by Hansen Hsu on 2025-09-24 
© Computer History Museum

Andy Hertzfeld was born in 1953 in Philadelphia, studied applied math and CS at Brown, and pursued a PhD in CS at Berkeley. After seeing the Apple II debut in 1977, he started writing, publishing and selling Apple II software. Hired by Apple in 1979 initially in the Apple II team, Hertzfeld befriended and aided Burrell Smith in the Macintosh team and eventually joined him there, becoming its second software engineer. Hertzfeld completed the port of QuickDraw from Lisa to Macintosh and wrote much of the Toolbox code and many desk accessories. Conflict with manager Bob Belleville contributed to Hertzfeld leaving Apple after the Macintosh launch. Afterwards, Hertzfeld developed Switcher, which allowed multitasking on the Macintosh for the first time, and helped organize the 1984 Hacker’s Conference.

recentItems.title: CHM Live | The Silicon Gold Rush: How AI is Driving the Development of New Chips
recentItems.description:
[Recorded August 27, 2026]
Are AI chips the new frontier of computing? What happens when the world’s biggest cloud companies stop buying chips and start designing their own?

In this program, we’ll unpack how companies once defined by software are now building custom silicon to run faster, cheaper, and at an unprecedented scale. The resulting competition is influencing global datacenter design and supply chains, marking a major new chapter in the evolution of AI.

What You’ll Experience:
-Demystify AI accelerators: what they are and why they’re so well-suited to modern machine learning workloads.
-Understand how custom silicon changes cloud economics, energy demands, data-center design, and business models.
-Hear directly from builders and insiders who are shaping the future of AI hardware, including Nvidia Chief Scientist and Senior Vice President of Research Bill Dally, Google VP and Technical Fellow Norm Jouppi, and CHM Fellow and UC Berkeley Pardee Professor of Computer Science Emeritus Dave Patterson.

Read our blog post: https://computerhistory.org/blog/the-silicon-gold-rush-how-ai-is-driving-development-of-new-chips/

recentItems.title: Oral History of James Pappas
recentItems.description:
Jim Pappas grew up in Western Massachusetts and attended local public high schools. Inspired initially by relatives in medicine, he originally pursued biology and accounting before joining the United States Air Force in 1975. Serving four years in precision calibration labs, he gained foundational technical experience—including early work on atomic clocks used for GPS testing—which sparked his passion for technology. Upon leaving the service, Pappas earned an electrical engineering degree with an emphasis in computer architecture in three years at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. 

Through a recommendation by professor Harold Stone, Pappas interned and subsequently took a full-time position at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC). Mentored by Ned Forrester, he built hardware emulators for video and graphics chips. Pappas went on to lead hardware engineering for the VT 200 series terminals alongside HT Cho, and developed 3D graphics chips for VAX and Alpha workstations. During a four-year stint building single-chip VAX CPUs, Pappas realized he had lost touch with the broader industry, prompting him to pivot toward industrywide interconnect standards. Collaborating with Intel, he helped rebrand and launch the Peripheral Component Interconnect (PCI) standard.

Joining Intel in 1994, Pappas spearheaded the development and deployment of Universal Serial Bus (USB) 1.0 to resolve PC cable complexity. By maintaining tight focus with a small consortium of key partners and tailoring features to anchor products (such as the Microsoft Mouse), USB achieved global ubiquity.

Following the success of USB, Pat Gelsinger recruited Pappas to oversee top technology initiatives across Intel’s desktop and data center divisions. Over his career, Pappas led or contributed to 77 major industry initiatives. Key efforts included:

USB 2.0: Driven by strict focus on digital imaging, storage, and communication.
NVMe & PCIe Interoperability: Partnering with leaders like Amber Huffman to bring PlugFests, ecosystem standards, and solid-state drive (SSD) adoption to mainstream platforms.
Compute Express Link (CXL): Serving as chair to unify competing memory architectures (CAPI, Gen-Z, CCIX) under a single open standard.
Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) & UALink: Establishing foundational open interconnect standards critical to modern AI architectures, chiplet integration, and pooled memory fabrics.

Throughout the interview, Pappas emphasizes leadership strategies for driving successful standards: keeping working groups small and focused, avoiding feature bloat, and embracing "creative insubordination". He attributes his career success to operating without fear of failure or termination, enabling decisive engineering and strategic risk-taking. Fully retired in Tumwater, Washington, Pappas reflects on his contribution to the memory and interconnect foundations powering today’s computing and AI landscapes.

Interviewed by Tom Coughlin on 2025-10-27 
© Computer History Museum

recentItems.title: Oral History of Eric Fullerton
recentItems.description:
Eric Fullerton is an Endowed Chair Professor at UCSD (University of California, San Diego) in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering and Chemical and Nanoengineering.  He also served as the Director of the Center of Memory and Recording Research (CMRR) at UCSD. After earning a PhD in physics from UCSD and working in a research position at Argonne National Laboratory, he joined IBM Almaden Research Center in 1997. 

There, he conducted groundbreaking research on developing synthetic antiferromagnetic structures in recording media, which led to their introduction into products and enabled higher areal density in thin-film magnetic media. Soon, all magnetic thin-film media worldwide used these advancements.  Derivations of these antiferromagnetically coupled structures continued to extend areal density and played a significant role in advancing thin-film magnetic recording media to this day. 

Eric Fullerton remained with HGST after Hitachi acquired IBM's Storage business in 2002, and in 2007 he joined the UCSD faculty.  This interview focuses on his work on antiferromagnetically coupled media but also covers his current research activities at CMRR and his own work in related areas such as spintronics. 

Interviewed by Tom Yamashita and Gerardo Bertero on 2025-10-20 
© Computer History Museum

recentItems.title: Oral History of John Chowning
recentItems.description:
Dr. John Chowning, is a pioneering composer and the inventor of FM synthesis. In this interview, Chowning details his key foundational ‘aha' moments, including using recursive structures in his 1977 composition Stria and accidentally discovering frequency modulation while researching quadraphonic audio spatialization. He describes the grueling, nocturnal nature of early timeshared computing at Stanford, which ultimately led to the founding of the Center for Computer Research in Music and Acoustics. 

Chowning reflects on his diverse musical trajectory, ranging from a childhood fascination with cave reverberation and playing jazz drums in the Navy to studying under Nadia Boulanger in Paris. Furthermore, he explores the massive commercial success and democratizing impact of the Yamaha DX7 synthesizer derived from his licensed patent, his work with the powerful Samson Box, and his eventual triumph over institutional skepticism within the traditional Stanford University music faculty department.  

Interviewed by Dag Spicer on 2026-02-10 
© Computer History Museum
